lessons.title: Meetings
lessons.tip: In business English, "follow up" and "action item" show up in almost every set of minutes.

items.translation: to check back on something later
items.example: I'll follow up with the client tomorrow.

items.translation: list of topics for a meeting
items.example: Let's stick to the agenda.
Can we reschedule to Thursday?
What was the outcome of the meeting?
Let's wrap up in five minutes.
Each action item needs an owner.

lessons.title: Everyday phrasal verbs
lessons.tip: A phrasal verb rarely means the sum of its parts. Learn each one like a new word.

items.example: I can't figure out this bug.
Stop putting off the dentist.
We ran out of coffee.
I'll look into it.
She came up with a great plan.
They get along really well.

lessons.title: Idioms
lessons.tip: Idioms make your English sound natural, but go easy on them in formal writing.

items.example: The exam was a piece of cake.
A joke helps to break the ice.
Let's make sure we're on the same page.
It's 7pm, let's call it a day.

items.term: the ball is in your court
items.example: I've sent the offer, the ball is in your court.

items.translation: to do something cheaply or carelessly
items.example: Don't cut corners on testing.

lessons.title: Commonly confused words
lessons.tip: Even native speakers mix these up. Spell-checkers won't save you.

items.example: The delay will affect the launch.
The change had a big effect.
This screw is loose.
Don't lose your keys.
Thanks for the compliment!
The wine is a nice complement to the meal.

lessons.title: Emails
lessons.tip: In a work email, short sentences and direct verbs sound more confident than hedging.

items.example: Please find attached the report.
As per our call, here are the details.

items.translation: to add someone to the conversation
items.example: Looping in Ana from finance.
Just a heads-up: the server goes down at 6.
Please reply at your earliest convenience.
Let's touch base next week.
